headline: Radio's first written use in Japanese is c. 1924, in a play called “Cherry Blossoms”.
“Bright” is probably a verb for “brighten” with an old adjective ending, first attested in 1689.
A weekday is a “plain day”, and the same spelling also hides a native compound.
The ring finger is the “medicine finger”, first cited in 1717.
A burn is a “burning place”, and the to of “place” voices to do.
The national border was already in the 706 record — and a native reading, kunizakai, sits behind the same spelling.
To gaze is related to “long” — possibly a “becoming long” — or to a “long watching” in the Kojiki.
“She” began as “that woman” — and only became a pronoun around 1888, under Western influence.
An “apartment” that is clipped — twice, from two different longer words.
“Eight days” is a classical やうか that was probably a やか first — or the other way round.
Kindergarten was, apparently, translated word for word from German — Japan's first ones opened in 1876.
To be finished is to be “done up” — and the 仕 is only there for its sound.
Dim is “thin dark” — with くらい voiced to ぐらい.
An instrument began as a “weapon” in 718 — and its look-alike 機械 became the common spelling from around 1874.
“To use” is “hold” plus “bring along”.
Cotton is “tree cotton”, worn down from mokumen to momen by 1560.
Zero could be English or French — and even the katakana word has a kanji spelling chosen by sound.
The twentieth of the month has two likely derivations — one through “twenty years old”.
Bushi is Chinese “warrior-man” — a theory that it once meant “bowing down” runs into the Nara period.
“Extreme” is the adverb “very” turned into an adjective.
To turn inside out is to “flip” the “back side” — かえす voiced to がえす.
A “boy” once meant a young person of either gender, “young years” in Chinese.
To smile is to “cheek-smile” — in kanji borrowed from a Chinese “slight smile”.
A senior is a Chinese “earlier fellow”, and ソンベ is its doublet.
A wallet is “wealth” plus “cloth” — a Japanese coinage found in texts from 1675.
“Cold” may be “claw” plus “painful”, with a missing i.
Hydrogen is “water element” — a word-for-word copy of Dutch, coined in 1834.
The youngest child is the “end child” — with a little clipped-off pause in the middle.
The word for an aunt is a “little mother” — and the kanji don't spell it that way.
A human being is, in Chinese, “people” plus “among”.
To refuse was originally to “split words”.
